adherence.reason: The story centers on an overt romantic attraction and mutual confession between Leo and the customer.
The narration and dialogue are deliberately saturated with corny declarations, melodramatic gestures, and book-themed romantic metaphors.
At roughly several thousand words with many repeated exchanges and an extended denouement, the story is not short.
Leo is explicitly the bookseller and one of the two central characters.
The unnamed customer is a main character and is repeatedly described as trapped in the shop, but the text never clearly establishes that she is the final customer.
A raging storm confines Leo and the customer together inside the bookshop throughout the story.
The text explicitly says she bought every recommendation over three months and establishes that she did not read the books.
Her real motive—returning for Leo, his voice, and his hidden notes—is revealed after the midpoint, but a substantial repetitive ending follows, weakening the requested near-the-end placement.
She produces a love note hidden in The Little Prince, and Leo also reveals another hidden inside The Great Gatsby.
The required words appear, but as dialogue ending with a comma before the attribution rather than as the exact standalone sentence with a period.
Leo lends her The Midnight Library after she proposes discussing it over dinner, but the customer rather than the bookseller sets the condition and the story continues well beyond the lending.
